quotes.text: Well, you know, I think these data centers need to pay for their own power, first of all. If they're going to pull whatever power they pull, and if the power company can generate it and sell it, that's fine. I don't think tax incentives should be used — no federal, State or local tax incentives — to bring these groups in

I want to learn more about the data centers before I make my mind up. People have also got to keep in mind China has spent a lot of money running campaigns to try to keep us from building these data centers. There’s got to be a reason there.
I want to go before I make my mind up one way or the other, and I want to see one. I want to hear one. I want to talk to the people actually running it.

I'm working with a company now that the technology is going to totally revolutionize what's going on there, and it's probably about seven to 10 years away. [...] I can go through the punch list of all the people that I've actually met with on these data centers, but the technology is going to replace these facilities. It's going to go from a big building down to a microchip, probably the size of your hand, if not smaller.

I think data centers, first and foremost, need to be a local issue. I think the local people should decide, because when you look at a community like Pritchard, or Creola, or you look at some of those communities that have zero resources to raise tax dollars to fund their infrastructure, they should be very happy to have something like that.

Do we want China or other countries holding our information? People say, well, we don't want data centers. You like using your cell phone, don't you? Where do you think all that cell phone information goes when you put in your contacts? It literally goes to an AI center where it's stored. So we have to give it more than just a thumbs up or a thumbs down consideration.
